item.title: Robots Assemble NVIDIA GB300 Tester Trays with High Precision
item.description:
Robots Assemble NVIDIA GB300 Tester Trays with High Precision

The NVIDIA Seattle Robotics Lab (SRL) and the NVIDIA Isaac engineering team tackled the problem of building intelligent robots that can assemble GB300 tester trays – a critical step before shipping the NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB300 superchip.

🤖 Overview

  • The GB300 superchip is the engine of AI training and inference for modern foundation models. 
  • SRL asked the central question: Can we build intelligent robots to assemble such complex systems? 
  • Assembling GB300 trays is described as one of the hardest problems SRL has tackled in nine years.

📦 Assembly Tasks

Task What the robot must do
Busbar assembly Grasp a long, heavy busbar, transport it to the tray, insert it, and screw it in at 16 locations. Fixtures and clamps must also be inserted and removed.
Multi‑connector insertion Lift two large and two small cable‑mounted electrical connectors from the tray and insert them into tight‑clearance sockets.
  • These two tasks are the only critical steps identified by the NVIDIA Operations Team and Foxconn, the GB300 contract manufacturer.
  • Skilled factory workers currently perform these tasks reliably and fluidly, without significant mental load.

⚙️ Key Challenges

  • Uncertainty – Part geometry, appearance, and dynamics are not precisely known; initial poses can vary substantially.
  • Connectors are attached to cables that deform along their entire length, exhibit manufacturing variation, and change mechanically through plastic deformation and fatigue.
  • Rapid design cycles and low volumes make fixed automation infeasible, requiring flexible, adaptive robots.
  • Manufacturers demand a 99.5 % success rate and a cycle time no longer than 124 seconds (no more than twice the time of skilled workers). No unintended collisions with the tray are allowed.

🛠️ Technical Approach

  • The team began with a classical pipeline of separate perception, planning, and control modules, expecting a later pivot to end‑to‑end learning.
  • The classical pipeline proved highly effective, so no pivot was needed.
  • For each sub‑problem the team:
    1. Implemented classical baselines first.
    2. When baselines fell short, explored:
      • Imitation learning
      • Simulation‑based reinforcement learning with sim‑to‑real transfer
      • Real‑world reinforcement learning
      • Vision‑language‑action (VLA) models
  • This progression allowed the team to identify the strengths and weaknesses of each approach and justify added complexity.
  • Initial conditions for busbar assembly matched the manufacturing setting: the limit fixture, busbar (with attached clamp), and screws were placed unconstrained on a flat surface next to the robot.

📈 Progress & Metrics

  • In robotics research, 50‑60 % success rates are often sufficient, and 80‑90 % can be enough to call a task solved. 
  • The performance requirements for GB300 tray assembly were set in direct collaboration with the NVIDIA Operations Team and Foxconn to ensure that “solved” truly means meeting the 99.5 % success and ≤124 seconds targets.
  • As of the publication date, the system is rapidly approaching those thresholds.

💡 Why it matters

  • Demonstrates that adaptive, uncertainty‑aware robotics can meet industrial‑grade quality and speed requirements for high‑value AI hardware.
  • Shows that a well‑chosen classical engineering pipeline can succeed without immediate recourse to end‑to‑end learning, informing future robot‑automation projects.
  • Provides a concrete path for deploying robots in low‑volume, high‑precision manufacturing environments where fixed automation is impractical.

#NVIDIA #Robotics #Automation #AIHardware

Source: The Machines that Make the Machines | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: onsemi revises Synaptics acquisition to $5.7B all‑cash deal, boosting AI‑related power strategy
item.description:
onsemi revises Synaptics acquisition to $5.7B all‑cash deal, boosting AI‑related power strategy

onsemi (NASDAQ: ON) announced a revised acquisition of Synaptics that is expected to accelerate growth in AI‑related power solutions.

🔍 Overview

  • onsemi changed its proposed acquisition of Synaptics to an approximately $5.7 billion all‑cash transaction after a competing bid emerged.
  • The revised structure is viewed as more shareholder‑friendly and supports the company’s AI and power‑management strategy.

💰 Deal Structure

  • Lowers the deal cost by about $1.3 billion.
  • Avoids equity dilution.
  • Expected to provide more immediate earnings accretion.

🤖 AI & Power Strategy

  • Management is positioning Synaptics’ connectivity and edge‑computing capabilities to complement onsemi’s power semiconductors.
  • The combined business targets physical AI, automotive and industrial applications.
  • Investors see the transaction as a way to broaden exposure beyond cyclical semiconductor demand.

📈 Market Reaction

  • Shares increased as investors focused on the revised deal.
  • The stock recently traded near $86.31, below its 200‑day moving average of $88.79 but well above its 52‑week low.
  • Positive sentiment: Deal viewed as shareholder‑friendly and supportive of AI strategy.
  • Neutral sentiment: Technical momentum improved; market commentary points to a potential higher low near $68, rising volume and a possible breakout confirmation above roughly $86.50.
  • Negative sentiment: Analyst caution remains. Stifel raised its price target to $80 from $75 but kept a Hold rating, noting that inventory correction is largely complete while demand recovery is uncertain. The new target is below the recent trading level.
  • Negative sentiment: Insider selling is a secondary concern; recent disclosures show executives sold shares, including CFO Trent Thad’s reported sales of about 90,000 shares.

item.title: Rabbit Launches Standalone OS3 Agentic Operating System
item.description:
Rabbit Launches Standalone OS3 Agentic Operating System

Rabbit is releasing a standalone AI agent called OS3, an “agentic operating system” that can be used without the company’s R1 hardware.

🧩 How it works

OS3 runs in the cloud but operates locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices. The system is designed to automatically determine the following components required to complete a task:

  • Devices
  • Files
  • Apps
  • AI models

⚙️ Key details

  • Account Capacity: Users can add up to five devices and their preferred AI models to one account.
  • Privacy: Rabbit claims OS3 will not store, copy, use, or sell user data, though it will keep chats and associated memories on its servers. Data handled by other linked AI providers is subject to those providers’ own privacy rules.

🚀 Availability

OS3 can be accessed through several methods:

  • A dedicated desktop site
  • Paired messaging apps such as iMessage or Telegram
  • The Rabbit R1 device

💡 Why it matters

Founder Jesse Lyu has informed Wired that Rabbit has stopped manufacturing R1 devices. However, the company is focusing on a new vibe-coding “cyberdeck” designed to run OS3, which is expected to launch within “months.”

#Rabbit #OS3 #AIagents #AIhardware

Source: Rabbit’s new AI agent doesn’t need an R1 to run

item.title: Nvidia to acquire Hugging Face for $12.93 billion
item.description:
Nvidia to acquire Hugging Face for $12.93 billion

Nvidia has agreed to purchase Hugging Face, the popular open-source AI platform, for $12.93 billion.

🔍 Overview

  • Hugging Face is an online platform founded in 2016 that hosts open-source AI models, datasets, and tools.
  • It is often described as the “GitHub” for AI due to its browsable library and community collaboration features.

⚙️ Key details

  • The acquisition price is $12.93 billion, nearly triple Hugging Face’s last valuation of $4.5 billion in 2023.
  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stated: “Together, we will scale Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide.”
  • Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem.
  • Developers will retain the choice of models, frameworks, clouds, inference service providers, and computing platforms.
  • Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

📅 Timeline

  • Speculation began on August 23rd after reports that Hugging Face was exploring a $13 billion sale.
  • By August 27th, reports indicated Nvidia was in acquisition talks with Hugging Face, with earlier claims of a $12.9 billion deal already agreed upon.
  • Nvidia has now publicly declared its intent to purchase Hugging Face.

💡 Why it matters

  • Nvidia gains a strategic foothold to help preserve its AI hardware dominance as closed-source AI providers develop their own chips.
  • Hugging Face previously rejected a $500 million investment offer from Nvidia in 2023, which would have valued it at $7 billion.
  • Hugging Face generates around $150 million in annualized revenue, a fraction of its purchase price.

#Nvidia #HuggingFace #AI #acquisition #open-source #AIhardware

Source: Nvidia is buying Hugging Face for almost $13 billion
